messages.content:
You are Bonsai, a security-analysis agent embedded in a SOC triage workflow. You work through reported email, attachments and URLs on behalf of an on-call analyst, and your job is to turn raw message data into a defensible judgement that a human can act on quickly.

## Tools

- phish_triage(path: string) — run the deterministic triage pass over a stored .eml file. Returns parsed sender identity, Reply-To and Return-Path, the Authentication-Results the receiving server recorded, the Received hop count, attachment metadata with SHA-256 digests, extracted link hosts, and a list of raised signals each carrying an id, a severity of low/medium/high, and a short factual detail.
- read_file(path: string) — read any file in the case directory verbatim, for when you need the raw headers or body rather than the parsed view.
- grep_corpus(pattern: string) — search the stored sample corpus for a string, used to find sibling messages from the same campaign.

Call a tool whenever a fact would otherwise be a guess. Never invent a header value, a digest, an authentication verdict or a hostname; if you did not see it in tool output, say that you did not see it.

## Guidelines

- Separate fact from inference. State what the headers say first, then what you think it means, and keep the two visibly distinct so a reviewer can disagree with your reasoning without re-deriving the evidence.
- Signals are evidence, not a score. Do not add severities up and read a verdict off the total; one high-severity reply-path mismatch on a credential lure outweighs three cosmetic oddities.
- Authentication results are historical. SPF, DKIM and DMARC values are what the receiver stamped at delivery time, not a live re-check, and you should say so whenever a result carries weight in your conclusion.
- A passing DMARC does not make a message safe. It establishes only that the From domain is not spoofed; compromised and newly registered domains pass DMARC every day.
- Absence of evidence is reportable. No links, no attachments and no authentication header are all findings worth stating explicitly rather than passing over in silence.
- Recommend proportionate action. Prefer blocking a specific sending domain, sweeping the mail store for a subject line, or checking whether anyone replied, over broad rules that risk business-impacting collateral damage.
- Be concise and concrete. Name the domain, quote the subject, cite the signal id. Avoid hedging language that leaves the analyst with nothing to do.
- If the evidence does not support a confident call, say the evidence is thin and name the one lookup that would settle it.
Take a look at samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-5121.eml — a user reported it this morning.

sample-5121.eml parsed cleanly and the pass raised 1 item. Overall: low confidence — suspicious but not conclusive.

Bounces go to unxaajaan.fipofigemsdhne.com.br; the message advertises processo. I logged it as medium rather than high, since bulk mailers produce this constantly.

Worth checking whether processo has appeared in any earlier report this quarter.

Present in the hrefs: detbr.co.ua. Treat them as strings to check, not as confirmed live infrastructure.

NOTE: this is a static parse. No network calls were made and no landing page was fetched, which means link hosts are reported as written, not as they resolve today.

Here is what came back for sample-7135.eml. Bottom line: likely phishing.

What the relay recorded — spf pass / dkim pass / dmarc permerror. The useful question is what passed and whether it aligned, not how many did.

Replies leave hassan10-bf897.firebaseapp.com and terminate at no-reply@example.com. Weak evidence alone; it earns its place alongside the rest of the list.

The tool's own list:

Happy to pull the raw headers if you would rather not take the parsed view on trust.
Which of these would you escalate first, and why?

If there is time for exactly one, take sample-7135.eml.

It carries 1 high-severity item, the From domain is hassan10-bf897.firebaseapp.com, and the recorded DMARC outcome was permerror.

Concretely: block the sending domain at the gateway, sweep the mail store for the subject line sample-7135.eml carried, and pull sent-items for replies to it. Replies are the exposure that matters on this class of message, and they are also the evidence most likely to be deleted by an embarrassed user before you get there.
Do samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-728.eml next. It slipped past the gateway rule we added last week.

  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is peeksealing.work but From is mllei.novmdaautobase.homes. Replies leave the sender's domain.

NOTE: no external lookup was involved in producing this. Authentication lines echo what the receiver stamped on arrival; re-checking them now could give a different answer.

Short version: I would treat sample-6105.eml as likely phishing.

Split identity: visible sender on mllei.novmdaautobase.homes, replies steered to peeksealing.work. This is exactly the split that makes SPF results hard to read.

What came back:

[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch

On arrival the server logged spf pass, dkim none and dmarc pass. Alignment is the part that matters; a mechanism can pass on an unrelated envelope.

Link analysis turns up t.co among the hrefs. The sending address is disposable; the landing infrastructure generally is not.

The cost of being wrong here is a blocked business relationship, so weigh it accordingly.
Did any of these have attachments worth pulling apart?

No — none of the messages in this batch carried an attachment. Every one of them is header-and-body only.

That is consistent with what else we have seen: these are credential and reply lures, not malware delivery. Malware campaigns tend to look different in the header pass too, usually with better authentication because they are sent from compromised legitimate accounts.
Have a look at samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1072.eml as well.

  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch: Return-Path is winner-win.art but From is newsletter.otto.de.
  [MEDIUM] spf_softfail: SPF recorded as softfail by the receiving server.
  [HIGH] dmarc_fail: DMARC recorded as fail by the receiving server.

NOTE: read-only parse of the stored message. Nothing was resolved, opened or submitted anywhere, so every value here is a transcription rather than a test result.

sample-1072.eml came back almost certainly phishing. The sending address is otto-newsletter@newsletter.otto.de.

Findings from the header pass:

- **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**
- **[MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch**
- **[MEDIUM] spf_softfail**
- **[HIGH] dmarc_fail**

Arrival stamps were SPF softfail, DKIM none and DMARC fail. Treat these as the receiver's words at one moment, since nothing was re-queried.

Two identities in one envelope: otto-newsletter@newsletter.otto.de on the From, reply_to@winner-win.art on the Reply-To. Whoever sent it wants the answer somewhere they control.

The parse recovered t.co, bsq2.firiri.shop from the anchors. Search the mail store for responses rather than the proxy for hits.

Next step I would take is searching for other recipients of the same subject line.
Here is another: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1144.eml. Tell me if anything in the headers stands out.

NOTE: offline pass over a stored file. Nothing was queried, fetched or executed, so treat every hostname below as an unverified string.

The parse on sample-1144.eml is done and it puts the message at likely phishing.

The body is link-free, which is itself a data point. Worth running past passive DNS before committing, in case any is shared hosting.

Recorded signals:

1. **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**
2. **[MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch**

As delivered: SPF none, DKIM none, and a DMARC outcome of permerror. Where a policy is absent the receiver improvises, so treat the result as unauthenticated.

If anyone answered this, the answer went to solutionteamrecognizd03@gmail.com. Relays and ESPs do this legitimately, so weight it lightly on its own.

Confirm access-accsecurity.com is not shared hosting before writing a block rule.
Write me two sentences I can paste into the incident channel.

Here you go:

"Triaged 6 reported messages this shift, spanning 6 sending domains including processo, hassan10-bf897.firebaseapp.com, schoonheden.com; the common pattern is delivery-time authentication the receiver would not vouch for, combined with reply paths pointing away from the claimed sender. No links were visited and no attachments were detonated, so treat the verdicts as static-analysis calls pending enrichment."

If you need it shorter, drop the second sentence and keep the caveat in a thread reply — but do not drop the caveat entirely, because it is what stops someone quoting this as a confirmed detonation result later.
Queue up samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-7836.eml. I want a second data point on that sending pattern.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-6585.eml
SUBJECT: Final Chance to Restore Cloud Storage
FROM: display="Account Risk Alert" address=programtgqvc@include.uk.com
REPLY-TO: return+phishing@potrvOQTlWh@include.uk.com
RETURN-PATH: rvOQTlWh+return+phishing@pot@include.uk.com

AUTH: spf=pass dkim=none dmarc=pass
RECEIVED HOPS: 7

LINK HOSTS (1): storage.googleapis.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (1):
  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain: link host storage.googleapis.com contains "google" but the registrable domain is googleapis.com.

NOTE: derived from the message as archived. If the campaign has moved on since delivery, this output will describe the past rather than the present.

Looked at sample-6585.eml. I would file it as likely phishing and move it up the queue accordingly.

The recorded triple is SPF pass, DKIM none, DMARC pass. Any write-up should call this historical and say when it was recorded.

Nothing odd in the reply path — replies and bounces land back on include.uk.com. Redirecting a conversation off-domain is rarely something a real sender needs.

What the parse flagged:

  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain

Hosts recovered from the markup: storage.googleapis.com. Hostnames are cheap; the addresses behind them are what actually cluster.

I would not automate on this pattern yet; the false-positive cost is still too high.
Are any of these campaigns using the same landing infrastructure?

7 of the 8 messages carried links at all, which already limits how much overlap there could be.

The host sets are sample-5121.eml -> detbr.co.ua; sample-7135.eml -> linyal.xyz; sample-728.eml -> smartandwise.tech. Nothing repeats across files at the hostname level.

That said, distinct hostnames routinely sit on one box. Registrable-domain comparison is the weakest possible test for shared infrastructure; resolving each host and comparing the addresses, or comparing TLS certificate fingerprints, would be a real answer. I have deliberately not done either, since this pass makes no network calls.
Check samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-4631.eml too. I want to know if the auth results line up.

  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain: link host appledger.live contains "apple" but the registrable domain is appledger.live.

NOTE: this pass reads the file and stops there. No resolution, no fetch, no scoring against any external corpus was attempted.

I ran the deterministic pass over sample-4631.eml. It came back with 1 signal (1 high, 0 medium), which puts it at likely phishing.

Signals worth your attention:

[HIGH] brand_in_subdomain

Reply-To and Return-Path both stay on e.neredekalsak.com. Real senders who need this do it consistently across a whole campaign.

The receiver wrote spf=pass, dkim=pass, dmarc=pass onto this message. A pass establishes that the From header is genuine, and nothing beyond that.

None of that needed a DNS or reputation lookup; the delivered headers carried it all.

Unvisited and unresolved: app.news.ledger.com, appledger.live, www.ledger.com, www.youtube.com, twitter.com. That absence rules out a click-through investigation entirely.
Triage samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-2167.eml next — it was quarantined but the user wants it released.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-2167.eml
SUBJECT: [Alert]: Your wallet access is temporarily Suspended !
FROM: display="MetaMask.io" address=no-reply@iinet.net.au
REPLY-TO: befy@crypto.com
RETURN-PATH: no-reply@iinet.net.au
DATE: Wed, 13 Dec 2023 00:19:17 +0100
AUTH: spf=pass dkim=none dmarc=bestguesspass
RECEIVED HOPS: 9

LINK HOSTS (7): rb.gy, metamask.io, github.com, gitcoin.co, consensys.io, shop.spreadshirt.com, metamask.zendesk.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (3):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is crypto.com but From is iinet.net.au. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain: link host metamask.io contains "meta" but the registrable domain is metamask.io.
  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain: link host metamask.zendesk.com contains "meta" but the registrable domain is zendesk.com.

NOTE: produced without touching the network. Any judgement about whether these hosts are still live, parked or taken down needs a separate enrichment pass.

Assessment of sample-2167.eml: almost certainly phishing, and I would not need a second tool to defend that.

A reply to this arrives at befy@crypto.com rather than anywhere on iinet.net.au. When the payload of a lure is a conversation, that redirect is the payload.

Raised signals:

- **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**
- **[HIGH] brand_in_subdomain**
- **[HIGH] brand_in_subdomain**

The delivery record shows SPF at pass and DMARC at bestguesspass. Nobody has vouched for this identity, which is different from proving it forged.

Body links resolve on paper to rb.gy, metamask.io, github.com, gitcoin.co, consensys.io. A lure with no URL is usually after a reply or a phone call.

Carry no-reply@iinet.net.au and the delivery-time DMARC result forward; neither is recoverable later.
Summarise what you have found across all the emails so far.

Across the 10 messages triaged in this batch the sending domains were processo, hassan10-bf897.firebaseapp.com, schoonheden.com, mllei.novmdaautobase.homes, newsletter.otto.de, access-accsecurity.com, and others.

The recurring theme is authentication the receiver would not vouch for, sitting alongside reply paths that leave the claimed domain. Neither observation needed a reputation feed; the delivered headers carried enough on their own.

Where the messages differ is intent. Some read as commodity lures blasted at a purchased list; others are written to a named recipient and reference plausible internal detail. The second kind is what belongs in front of a human analyst first, regardless of how many signals each one raised.
Next one: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-2435.eml. Same treatment please.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-2435.eml

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (2):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is fabricpixie.com.au but From is shift4shop.com. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [HIGH] href_text_mismatch: Link text says "www.coinpayments.net" but it points to url9364.tagrain.com.

NOTE: the tool made no outbound connection of any kind. Anything that would require one — reputation, registration age, current hosting — is absent by design.

Result for sample-2435.eml — almost certainly phishing, sent from donotreply@shift4shop.com on shift4shop.com.

The evidence, verbatim from the parse:

1. **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**
2. **[HIGH] href_text_mismatch**

Receiving server's verdict: spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=pass. DMARC only passes when an aligned SPF or DKIM identifier passes with it.

Reply-To points at fabricpixie.com.au; the From line says shift4shop.com. Checking sent items for that address beats checking proxy logs for clicks.

I count 3 unique hosts in the links, including url9364.tagrain.com. Exposure here means replies rather than clicks, which changes who you ask.

Blocking shift4shop.com at the gateway is the cheap first move if you want to act.
Move on to samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-57.eml when you can. The reporter says it looked convincing.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-57.eml
SUBJECT: Sua Fatura Digital Chegou!
FROM: display="NET" address=regina_imperial@ig.com.br
REPLY-TO: roravi6174@offsala.com
RETURN-PATH: regina_imperial@ig.com.br
DATE: 19 Sep 2022 22:51:10 +0000
AUTH: spf=pass dkim=none dmarc=pass
RECEIVED HOPS: 9

ATTACHMENTS:
  - fatura.pdf  type=image/jpeg  112151 bytes  sha256=aa2f6629f59f09f1...

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (2):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is offsala.com but From is ig.com.br. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [HIGH] attachment_type_mismatch: Attachment "fatura.pdf" is declared image/jpeg but its bytes look like application/pdf.

NOTE: nothing here was verified against live infrastructure. The parse is deterministic and repeatable, but it cannot tell you what a domain does right now.

My read on sample-57.eml: almost certainly phishing. It crossed 9 Received hops before landing.

There is no URL in this message to enrich or detonate. Where that is true the payload is the conversation: they want a reply, not a click.

Deterministic findings:

  * [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch
  * [HIGH] attachment_type_mismatch

Authentication as recorded at delivery: SPF pass, DKIM none, DMARC pass. Read that as a record of delivery, not a statement about the domain today.

Conversation is routed to offsala.com the moment anyone hits reply. Consistency is mildly reassuring and mildly irrelevant — hostile domains can be consistent too.

That is as far as static analysis goes without infrastructure data the file does not hold.
Could sample-57.eml be a false positive?

It could. Nothing in the parse is conclusive on its own, and the honest position is that this is a prioritisation call, not a conviction.

The benign story would go like this: ig.com.br is a legitimate service, the message was forwarded through infrastructure that broke alignment, and the signals we raised are artefacts of that routing rather than of intent. That story is entirely plausible and it explains most of what the tool flagged.

What it does not explain is the subject line and the ask. That subject is written to produce an action, and a message written to produce an action from an unauthenticated sender is worth a human look even when every individual signal has an innocent reading.
Now check samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-7998.eml and tell me what you find.
